extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, interpreting, and rejecting claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/(f) (pre-AIA §112 sixth paragraph) including common indefiniteness pitfalls and form-paragraph uses. Focused on examiner evaluation of claim language and appropriate Office action language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Are a Literal Translation
rubrics_metrics.description: This paragraph should only be used where the specification does not clearly redefine the claim term at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when claims appear to be literal translations with grammatical/idiomatic errors and the specification does not provide a clear definition for the claim term. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Term - Term of Degree Rendering Claim Indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The term "[1]" in claim [2] is a relative term which renders the claim indefinite. The term "[1]" is not defined by the claim, the specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree, and one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of the scope of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain in bracket 3 which parameter, quantity, or other limitation is rendered indefinite by the relative term. This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite Claim Language: "For Example"
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding claim [1], the phrase "for example" renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitation(s) following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d). This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Range/Limitation And Narrow Range/Limitation in Same Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad range or limitation together with a narrow range or limitation that falls within the broad range or limitation (in the same claim) may be considered indefinite if the resulting claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the patent protection desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether the narrower language is (a) merely exemplary (and thus not required) or (b) a required feature. Use when the claim recites both broad recitation [2] and narrower statement [3] in the same claim. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite Claim Language: "Or The Like"
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding claim [1], the phrase "or the like" renders the claim(s) indefinite because the claim(s) include(s) elements not actually disclosed (those encompassed by "or the like"), thereby rendering the scope of the claim(s) unascertainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d). This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite Claim Language: "Such As"
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding claim [1], the phrase "such as" renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite MPEP § 2173.05(d). This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Steps Omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential steps, such omission amounting to a gap between the steps. The omitted steps are: [2]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2, recite the steps omitted from the claims. Give the rationale for considering the omitted steps critical or essential, explaining the basis for concluding the inventor regards the omitted matter as essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Must Be Structurally Clear and One-Sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim(s) are narrative in form and replete with indefinite language. The structure which goes to make up the device must be clearly and positively specified. The structure must be organized and correlated in such a manner as to present a complete operative device. The claim(s) must be in one sentence form only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use format of claims in cited patents as examples. Narrative/multisentence claims or claims lacking organized correlated structure may be indefinite and subject to rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure To Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim - Omnibus Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite in that it fails to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language. This claim is an omnibus type claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. Use to reject an 'omnibus' type claim (example: "A device substantially as shown and described."). No further explanation is necessary. In bracket 2, recite the steps omitted from the claims when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark or Trade Name as a Limitation in the Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] contains the trademark/trade name [2]. Where a trademark or trade name is used in a claim as a limitation to identify or describe a particular material or product, the claim does not comply with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that trademark identifies source, not the goods, and thus does not properly identify/describe goods. In bracket 2 insert the trademark and its location in the claim; in bracket 3 specify the material/product identified; give rationale for considering the omitted steps or identified matter critical or essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Elements Omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the elements. The omitted elements are: [2]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2 recite the omitted elements and give rationale explaining why the inventor regards the omitted matter as essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Cooperative Relationships Omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the necessary structural connections. The omitted structural cooperative relationships are: [2]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejection must be preceded by form paragraph 7.30.02 or 7.103. In bracket 2, recite omitted structural cooperative relationships and give the rationale for considering them critical or essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) Applies When 'Means' or 'Step' Is Used
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term 'means' or 'step' and includes functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure, material or acts necessary to perform the recited function. If an examiner finds that 'means' is used but prong (B) or (C) of the 3-prong analysis is not met, the Office action must explain why a limitation using 'means' or 'step' is not being treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f). Cite TriMed, Altiris and other precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) Does Not Apply When 'Means' Not Used (Rebuttable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that does not use the term 'means' will trigger the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should nonetheless consider whether the presumption is overcome (i.e., the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or else recites function without sufficient structure). Cite Phillips, CCS Fitness, Personalized Media. Even without 'means', terms can be construed under 112(f) if they are generic placeholders or otherwise lack structural meaning (e.g., 'module', 'mechanism for').

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-Prong Analysis to Determine Invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation if it meets the following 3-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the term 'means' or 'step' or a term used as a substitute for 'means' that is a generic placeholder; (B) the term is modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or similar); and (C) the term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim limitation meets all three prongs, it should be treated under 112(f). If unclear whether limitation falls within 112(f), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) may be appropriate. The examiner must expressly state in the Office action when a 35 U.S.C. 112(f) interpretation is applied. If the limitation uses 'means' but prongs (B) or (C) are not met, explain why 112(f) is not applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of Generic Placeholders That May Invoke 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-structural generic placeholders that may invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) include 'mechanism for', 'module for', 'component for', 'element for', 'member for', 'apparatus for', 'machine for', 'system for' (list not exhaustive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fixed list; each case turns on its facts. Consider whether the term acts as a generic placeholder (black-box) lacking structural meaning. Cite Welker Bearing, Mass. Inst. of Tech., Personalized Media, Mas-Hamilton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Modification Requirement (Prong B)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'means' or 'step' or the generic placeholder must be modified by functional language (typically linked by 'for' or another linking word or phrase such as 'configured to' or 'so that').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A function must be recited within the claim limitation; the mere use of 'means' with no associated function rebuts invocation. A statement of function only in the preamble is generally insufficient. For process claims, step-plus-function is implicated only when steps plus function without acts are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient Structure/Material/Acts Rebuttal (Prong C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'means' or generic placeholder must not be modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function in order to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f). If the claim itself recites sufficient structure or acts, 112(f) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural modifiers (e.g., 'detent mechanism', 'circuit') or explicit acts may impart sufficient structure. Use case law (Envirco, Rodime, Cole, Unidynamics) to assess whether the recited language supplies sufficient structure. If a structural modifier further describes the generic placeholder, it may avoid 112(f) treatment; conversely, non-structural modifiers will not.

rubrics_metrics.name: How To Determine Whether a Term Denotes Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners may check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject-matter-specific dictionaries provide evidence that the term has achieved recognition as a noun denoting structure; and/or (3) the prior art provides evidence that the term is an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Ex parte Rodriguez (precedential) and relevant Federal Circuit precedent. Consider whether common art usage or the specification gives the term structural significance (e.g., 'filters', 'circuit', 'brakes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Office Action Requirements When Applying 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination that a claim is being interpreted according to 35 U.S.C. 112(f) should be expressly stated in the examiner's Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner determines 'means' is used but prong (B) or (C) is not met, the Office action must explain why the limitation is not being treated under 112(f). If 112(f) is asserted and applicant objects, applicant may present a showing of sufficient structure or amend the claim to recite sufficient structure to avoid 112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant Options in Response to 112(f) Finding
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to an Office action finding that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is invoked, applicant may: (1) present a sufficient showing to establish that the claim limitation recites sufficient structure to perform the claimed function; or (2) amend the claim limitation to avoid interpretation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (e.g., by reciting sufficient structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant does not want the limitation interpreted under 112(f), they must either add structure in the claim or rebut the presumption by showing the limitation already recites sufficient structure. If unclear whether 112(f) applies, a rejection under 112(b) may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process Claims and Step-Plus-Function Caution
rubrics_metrics.description: For process claims, step-plus-function treatment is implicated only when steps plus function without acts are present; merely using '-ing' verbs like passing, heating, reacting, transferring etc. does not automatically create step-plus-function limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overbroadly converting typical process language into step-plus-function limitations. Cite O.I. Corp., Baran and related precedents. The claimed function must lack associated acts to be step-plus-function.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Absolutes — Fact-Specific Determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no fixed list of words that always result in 35 U.S.C. 112(f) interpretation; every case will turn on its own unique set of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must carefully consider the term in light of the specification and commonly accepted meaning in the technological art. Use precedential cases as guidance but apply to the specific facts of the application.
